title: The Stones on the Road
summary: A man clears his field by tossing the stones onto everyone's road, and laughs at the pious man who warns him. Years later he trips over his own stones and understands that what belongs to everyone belongs to him too. A gentle story about caring for shared spaces.
pages: In a certain village there lived a man who had a big field. The field was full of stones: small ones and big ones, round ones and pointy ones. "How can I plant wheat here?" the man grumbled. "My plow keeps getting stuck!" So he decided to clear the field, stone by stone.

He picked up a stone and threw it... onto the road beside the field. And another stone, and another. Everyone in the village walked along that road: children running to play, women with baskets, old men with walking sticks. And now the road was filling up with stones.

A pious man, a kindhearted man who always thought of others, passed by and saw. He stopped and asked, "Why are you clearing stones from ground that isn't yours onto ground that is yours?" In other words: "Why are you taking stones out of the place that isn't yours, and putting them in the place that is?"

The man burst out laughing. "What nonsense are you talking?" he said. "This field is mine! And the road isn't mine at all, it belongs to everyone!" He shrugged and went on throwing stones. And the pious man? He just shook his head and went on his way.

A few years went by. The man had hard times, and he didn't have enough money. He had to sell his field to someone else. Now he had no field at all. But the road? It was still there, for him and for everyone.

One day the man was walking along that same road, lost in thought. Suddenly, oops! His foot struck a stone, and he tripped and fell on his knees. He got up, brushed the dust off his clothes and rubbed his knee. Then he looked down and saw... his own stones! The very same stones he had thrown from his field.

The man stood there for a long time. "That pious man spoke well," he whispered to himself. Now he understood: the field was his for only a short time, and now it belongs to someone else. But the road that belongs to everyone is his too, always. When he made it messy, he made his own place messy.

The man bent down, picked up one stone and set it aside. And another, and another. A boy passing by asked, "What are you doing?"
The man smiled: "I'm clearing my road, and yours too."

We have places that belong to everyone, too: the kindergarten, the playground, the sidewalk, the beach. When we throw a wrapper in the trash and not on the ground, or pick up a bottle someone forgot, we take care of a place that is ours too. Because what belongs to everyone belongs to us as well.
